title: The Treasury Has Survived the Second Great War
subtitle: Turn-based strategy, cards and role-playing

opening.title: A Coalition Cannot Pay You in Exposure
paragraphs: “Nigga, why is your chair listed as a vehicle?” Tank asked.

The hotel manager had delivered the financial statement in a folder thick enough to qualify as supporting furniture. We had found the agenda, recovered the pen, and agreed to discuss money before the evening grew any more ceremonial. I had responded by taking my seat in a mechanical photo throne. Its footrest extended into the exact place the catering staff needed to walk. Even my sitting down had logistical consequences.

“It's powered,” I explained. “So is a vacuum,” Rae said. “One of those would help.” She had returned from showing Nia her bike and looked unusually pleased with a discussion of brake cables. Nia looked pleased too. Neither had submitted a report. I respected their privacy by waiting almost twelve seconds before suggesting a commemorative photograph. Shawna squeezed my shoulder until my interest in documentation subsided.

The second room offered strategy games, card battles, long role-playing stories, and enough imaginary governments to support my worst instincts. I had printed place cards for ministries. Rae's said Practical Affairs. Kit's said Cultural Affairs. Nia's said Legal Affairs. Shawna looked at the last word and asked whether her ministry could be Private Affairs, beginning with my immediate removal from public office. I assured her my domestic portfolio remained exceptionally strong. “Your portfolio was late to its appointment,” she said. Tank studied the invoice harder, out of respect for a man dying in office.

Velvet put her actual contract beside the ministries. She had a costume rack, a rehearsed number, and a fee that didn't become less real because I called the evening a coalition. Remy wanted his microphone checked and his fanfare left gloriously ridiculous. Mercedes wanted her own set and recording arrangements honored. Porsche wanted nobody borrowing her equipment in exchange for gratitude. Rosa wanted staff time paid. Those were concrete requests. My request concerned being photographed beneath a large symbolic eagle nobody remembered approving.

Mika loved the eagle. “It would look incredible over the stage.” I pointed at them triumphantly. “But we don't have the rigging or the money,” they continued. The betrayal arrived with professional measurements. They put their tiny model hotel on the table and began using coins to represent possible costs. It was the first casino activity that had frightened me before anybody placed a bet.

June and Dez arrived carrying the Blue Comet folder. The jacket came too, over Dez's arm. June identified it as her asset before she sat down. Dez identified her alterations as a long-term investment. Their 1967 peace arrangement had apparently failed because each believed the other had refused to sign. Both now wanted the current summit to recognize their excellent record of reasonable behavior. I understood the emotional appeal of a committee certifying whatever story made you look best.

Nia declined to certify either veteran's entire life. She would help read the old paper during the break. For now she wanted clear terms for this evening and then freedom to be a guest. Rae moved the good crackers within her reach without interrupting her sentence. Kit slid a lamp toward them, then reclaimed it an inch because she needed light on her own notes too. Nobody disappeared into service. Everybody kept a chair.

Dre sat down with his casserole and claimed the blue controller he'd brought. His Crip affiliation didn't make him my Minister of Blue Lighting, a position he declined before I finished explaining it. Darnell offered to underwrite entertainment from future yacht income. Velvet asked whether future money could arrive before present soundcheck. Darnell looked toward the bar, where his economic theory faced fewer follow-up questions.

I wanted to tell everyone that turn-based games meant a peaceful room. Shawna tapped the thick financial statement. “This waits while you think. Does it feel simple?” Fair. Waiting gave us time to understand decisions; it didn't remove the decisions. The useful game notes would remain plain, so a person could choose an appealing challenge without having me convert patience into a promise of ease.

I raised the ceremonial pen. Nia handed me an ordinary pencil. “Until we agree on the numbers.” The mechanical chair lowered itself with a squeak that sounded expensive. Tank caught my glass. Rosa moved the catering trolley past my newly humbled knees. Nigga, the treasury had opened for business, and its first order was getting my ass out of the aisle.

games.case_title: The Capital Has Four Fountains and No Change
scene: Civilization VI encouraged me to describe the summit budget as an emerging nation. I pointed at the four decorative fountains on the rental sheet. “Public infrastructure.”
Rosa pointed at the unpaid extra staff hours. “Public embarrassment.” Tank leaned over the page. “Nigga, your civilization discovered waterfalls before wages.”

Kit wanted one fountain moved away from her music stand because its cheerful gurgling competed with every quiet note. Rae wanted the same fountain emptied before somebody knocked it over beside the signing table.

I argued that capitals needed grandeur. Nia asked whether grandeur had a receipt we could cancel. Mika admitted the fountains looked beautiful, then identified two we could return without dismantling half the room.
June offered to name the remaining pair after herself and Dez. Dez said naming something after her didn't satisfy a debt, especially if it mostly leaked.

We returned two fountains. The staff line became payable. I announced the first reform of my administration. Shawna wrote CARRIED THE FOUNTAIN beside my name, which was historically precise and politically devastating.
games.pleasure: Build a civilization across a large sweep of history, choosing how cities grow, what people research and how to deal with neighboring powers. The appeal is seeing many small decisions create a society with a recognizable direction rather than following one prescribed storyline.
games.burden: District placement, research, policies, diplomacy and multiple units produce heavy menu and planning demands. Single-player turns permit deliberation, but this is emphatically not cognitively simple because it is turn-based. Avoid assuming online turn settings match solo play; held map gestures and interface readability still need a trial.
games.first: Use the guided opening or a modest single-player start to found one city and make one production choice. Judge whether the explanations make that decision interesting before opening an empire's worth of additional responsibilities.
games.ruling: The empire-building scope can be rewarding when its planning appeals; waiting turns do not simplify it. Our capital has achieved payroll by reducing its unnecessary population of fountains.
games.source_note: Exact base-game PC listing supports districts, research, policies and diplomacy. Waits refers to single-player turn decisions; complete input comfort and multiplayer timer/co-op configurations are not verified.
games.title: Sid Meier's Civilization VI
games.quick_pitch: Build a civilization whose cities, discoveries, and relationships reflect your decisions, gradually creating a history with a direction of your own.
games.what_you_do: Found a city, choose its production or research, and manage units, districts, policies, and relationships with neighboring powers over successive turns.
games.watch_for: Solo turns allow deliberation, but menus and planning are heavy; test map gestures and readability rather than assuming cognitive simplicity.

games.case_title: The Dynasty Has Inherited a Cardigan
scene: Old World's family politics made June argue that the Blue Comet jacket debt should be treated as a dynastic matter. Dez asked whether decades of alterations entitled her heirs to a sleeve.
“Your heirs can inherit the cardigan,” June said. “My aunt liked that cardigan,” Dez replied. “Then your aunt can adjudicate, nigga.”
I offered to establish a hereditary Ministry of Restitution. Nia asked whether I intended to pay its salaries. Suddenly I admired a smaller government.

Rae examined the photograph of the original jacket. She liked the stitching across the shoulder. Dez began explaining how she'd altered it, and Kit leaned closer because she'd never seen a lining like that.
June listened, pretending not to. When Dez described the final fitting, June remembered which song had been playing. They disagreed about the song but remembered the same ridiculous dance step.
Shawna touched my knee beneath the table. “That's a dynasty.” I nodded like I understood, then offered to order a crest. “Nigga,” she said, and the noble house survived without merchandise.
games.pleasure: Old World combines historical strategy with a living dynasty: rulers age, families compete, children grow and personal events affect the state. People and relationships can give empire management a more intimate story than a map of anonymous production totals.
games.burden: The developer declares play without timed input, a mouse-only option and saving at any time. That is encouraging for pacing, while court relationships, cities, resources and character roles still make this a dense strategy game. Declared co-op exists, but its setup and shared responsibilities require a separate check.
games.first: Follow the introductory guidance until one ruler faces one clear decision. Read the affected person's name and consequence, then decide whether that personal layer makes the surrounding management enjoyable or merely adds another spreadsheet to remember.
games.ruling: The dynasty's personal events may make empire management attractive, with its dense systems understood. Our inherited claim concerns one jacket, one cardigan, and a remarkably durable shared memory.
games.source_note: Exact listing supports dynasties/families and declares no timed input, Mouse Only Option, Save Anytime and co-op. Those declarations do not establish low menu load or a personally comfortable multiplayer arrangement.
games.title: Old World
games.quick_pitch: Guide a historical dynasty where aging rulers, competing families, and personal events give empire management a continuing story about people.
games.what_you_do: Read a ruler's decision, consider its personal consequences, and manage cities, resources, character roles, and court relationships as the dynasty develops.
games.watch_for: Untimed input is declared, but cities and family relationships form a dense strategy game; co-op setup needs separate checking.

games.case_title: The Ministry Has Changed Its Outfit Again
scene: HUMANKIND's changing cultures inspired my declaration that the summit could evolve beyond its first identity. Velvet looked at my new ceremonial jacket. “You mean your fourth outfit.”
“Adaptation.” “Dry-cleaning liability.”

Mika wanted to move from welcome mode to actual evening mode. Kit wanted the stage colors changed for karaoke. Rae wanted the budget to recognize that good snacks remained good snacks regardless of historical era.

June said the Blue Comet had reinvented itself three times in one summer. Dez remembered the same jukebox in every version. “New sign. Same nigga hogging the buttons.” June smiled proudly, taking this as evidence of continuity.

Nia revised the proposed ministries into temporary jobs with specific endings. Velvet became the person approving her own costume handling. Rosa retained catering authority because she'd already been doing it successfully.
I asked what I became. Shawna held up the jacket bag. “A husband who can put his old clothes away.” My civilization entered a new era carrying its previous era over one arm.
games.pleasure: Shape a civilization by combining cultures across eras rather than staying with a single identity throughout history. City growth, fame and tactical conflicts turn the map into an account of accumulated decisions, including choices about what kind of achievements matter.
games.burden: Empire management and battlefield decisions sit on top of one another. Culture transitions add systems to learn, while resources, diplomacy and competing goals make the memory load high. Turn-based battles do not establish a universally simple control scheme or relaxed multiplayer timer settings; begin with solo play and inspect menus.
games.first: Follow the early guidance through one development choice and read what it changes. Stop to decide whether comparing those possibilities feels engaging before treating the next historical era as an obligation to keep playing.
games.ruling: The changing-culture structure offers a distinctive historical strategy, with its management burden intact. Our summit's latest era has replaced ceremonial titles with jobs that end when their work does.
games.source_note: Publisher listing supports combining cultures, fame and turn-based tactical battles. Pacing label applies to solo strategic decisions; complete holds, map controls and multiplayer configurations remain unchecked.
games.title: HUMANKIND
games.quick_pitch: Combine cultures across historical eras, shaping a civilization whose cities, conflicts, and achievements reflect an accumulating series of different choices.
games.what_you_do: Choose developments, manage resources and diplomacy, and make battlefield decisions while adapting the civilization to changes across successive historical eras.
games.watch_for: Empire and battlefield systems overlap, making memory demands high; solo turns do not establish relaxed settings in every configuration.

games.case_title: The Mech Has Moved the Dessert Table
scene: Into the Breach showed attacks before they landed. I wished the hotel did that with invoices. Mika pointed out that the rental company had sent me six clear estimates.
“Nigga, those were telegraphed,” Tank said. “You ignored the telegram.”
Rosa needed a path from the kitchen. Remy's costume trunk occupied one square, Kit's lamp another, and my ceremonial chair occupied enough territory to govern itself.
Rae sketched the room on a napkin. One move: chair against the wall. Another: trunk beside the stage. Suddenly the dessert trolley could pass without threatening a crown or a kneecap.

Mika liked the rearrangement so much they added a tiny model chair to their miniature hotel. Kit objected that the real lamp's new angle improved Velvet's entrance more than hers. Velvet offered to trade the angle after her show.
I attempted to move my chair with dignity. Its wheels squeaked through the entire negotiation. Shawna followed carrying my abandoned sash. The giant machine in this battle was my fucking furniture.
games.pleasure: Small mech battles become visible tactical puzzles because enemy attacks are telegraphed before the next turn. The pleasure is finding an unexpected move that changes several threats at once, often by shifting positions rather than simply choosing the strongest attack.
games.burden: A compact board can still ask for demanding spatial reasoning. Protecting buildings, understanding attack direction and managing limited actions are central, and failure changes a run. The turn structure supports thought before acting; it does not prove every menu or selection gesture suits the player. Advanced Edition adds more systems.
games.first: Try the opening guidance and inspect one announced enemy attack before choosing a move. Say which square is threatened and what one action changes; there is no need to solve the entire campaign to test that central pleasure.
games.ruling: The visible tactical problems may appeal to careful planning, while the practical notes govern the trial. Our napkin battle succeeded by relocating one oversized chair instead of buying another solution.
games.source_note: Publisher describes minimalistic turn-based combat with telegraphed attacks; current PC includes Advanced Edition content. Waits reflects tactical decision structure, not a complete no-hold/comfort certification.
games.title: Into the Breach
games.quick_pitch: Solve small mech battles by reading enemy attacks in advance, finding a move that changes several threats through clever positioning.
games.what_you_do: Inspect the next announced attack, identify threatened squares, and move or act with a mech to change what will happen.
games.watch_for: The small board still demands spatial reasoning and limited-action planning; selection controls need testing, and failure changes a run.

games.case_title: The Displaced Queen Has a Better Fanfare
scene: Wargroove's displaced queen needed allies. Velvet needed the electrical socket beneath my ceremonial chair. I considered these parallel struggles and offered a formal alliance.
She pointed. “Move your throne, nigga.” Diplomacy was becoming terribly specific.

Remy proposed a joint entrance with his fanfare leading into her number. Kit challenged the key. Mercedes tested the transition at the piano while the rest of us waited to discover whether monarchy could hear pitch.
It actually worked. Remy looked delighted. Velvet adjusted one note, he adjusted his bow, and the alliance gained a musical border neither objected to.
Rae moved the extension cable away from the signing table. Nia held it clear while she worked. I offered strategic commentary until Shawna asked me to be the infantry carrying the chair.

We parked it against the wall. June sat in it instantly. “Better than the Blue Comet chairs.” Dez asked whether she'd borrowed this one too. The queen had been restored, but the historic opposition retained its seat directly beside her.
games.pleasure: Wargroove gives turn-based army battles a bright fantasy cast and a campaign about a displaced queen seeking allies. Commanders have distinctive special abilities, while different units and terrain make each map a problem about positioning and resource choices.
games.burden: Managing an army, its funds and its unit matchups is more involved than moving one character. The editor and multiplayer add separate layers rather than simplifying the campaign. Co-op is listed, but exact campaign coverage and setup should be checked; no untimed or hold-free claim applies automatically to every configuration.
games.first: Start with the campaign's opening instruction and command one unit through one explained action. Test the map selection interface and the clarity of the unit information before recruiting a large army or opening the editor.
games.ruling: The fantasy campaign and commander personalities can make tactics appealing, with unit and interface demands retained. Our musical alliance found its socket by expelling the host's throne from useful territory.
games.source_note: Exact PC listing supports turn-based campaign, commander Grooves and native co-op categories. Co-op mode scope is not assumed to cover the whole main campaign; complete input demands are unchecked.
games.title: Wargroove
games.quick_pitch: Lead a displaced queen's bright fantasy campaign, using distinctive commanders and varied terrain to make positioning and resource choices matter.
games.what_you_do: Follow campaign instructions, select units on the map, and choose movement or attacks while managing funds and different army roles.
games.watch_for: Army funds and unit matchups require learning; exact co-op coverage, timing settings, and selection gestures need their own check.

games.case_title: Forbidden Technology Is a Jukebox with Bluetooth
scene: Wargroove 2's forbidden technology led June to inspect the wireless music tablet with suspicion. She wanted her Blue Comet song queued. Dez wanted evidence that it would play only once.
I offered a password-protected accord. Mika said we could simply put the song in the set list. My treaty provisions were losing to buttons again.
Remy asked whether his revised fanfare counted as new technology. Velvet said it counted as a persistent condition. He played the opening anyway, softer, and she smiled before she could stop herself.

Kit wanted a clean transition into karaoke. Mercedes wrote the order on a card: song, number, break, karaoke. Four lines resolved a conflict I had planned to announce beneath a projection of crossed swords.
June approved until she saw her song appeared only once. Dez tapped the card. “Reparations begin with restraint, nigga.”

I quietly deleted the crossed swords from the slideshow. Mika caught me, then admitted they looked excellent. We saved them for an optional photograph, where forbidden technology could harm only my dignity.
games.pleasure: The sequel builds a new conflict around forbidden technology and several connected campaigns, with new commanders and a revised Groove system. Its attraction is returning to colorful map tactics with fresh factions, tactical possibilities and a continuing fantasy world.
games.burden: New commander abilities and linked campaigns add knowledge to the familiar army-management demands. The separate Conquest mode and editing tools are optional avenues, not recommended first steps here. Native co-op is listed, but campaign coverage, timing settings and comfortable selection controls need their own verification.
games.first: Take the initial campaign instruction one action at a time and read one commander's ability carefully. Compare that single mechanic with ordinary movement before exploring extra modes or designing an ambitious custom scenario for everyone else.
games.ruling: The sequel adds factions and abilities to an already tactical structure; those additions still require learning. Our forbidden jukebox technology has been restrained by a four-line card and Dez's finger.
games.source_note: Current publisher listing supports three campaigns, revised Grooves, Conquest and native co-op. Waits refers to turn-based tactics, not an all-modes or hold-free guarantee.
games.title: Wargroove 2
games.quick_pitch: Return to colorful army tactics through linked campaigns, new commanders, and a conflict over forbidden technology in an expanding fantasy world.
games.what_you_do: Read a commander's ability, move units, and use battlefield actions while learning the revised Groove system through the initial campaign.
games.watch_for: New abilities add knowledge to army management; extra modes and listed co-op do not automatically simplify campaign play.

games.case_title: The Land, Sea, and Air Budgets Are Mostly Snacks
scene: Advance Wars gave me three branches for our imaginary ministries. Land would cover seating. Sea would cover drinks. Air would cover the chandelier rental. Nia waited until I finished admiring the symmetry.
“Where are the performers?” “Culture.” “You've invented a fourth ministry to avoid paying the first three correctly.”

Tank volunteered for Sea and immediately requested a water refill. Rae claimed Land long enough to reject the decorative chairs nobody could sit on. Kit asked whether Air included stage lighting or just my emotional atmosphere.
Mika drew three columns on a sheet and wrote actual costs beneath them. The chandeliers overwhelmed their branch before the first skirmish. I tried declaring emergency powers.
Shawna vetoed the phrase emergency powers. Velvet seconded her. Remy played a tiny defeat sound, then apologized to the sound for being too effective.
We abandoned the ministries and kept Mika's cost columns. Nigga, my armed forces had dissolved into an ordinary budget, leaving the admiral holding two glasses of water and a very good sandwich.
games.pleasure: This Switch collection rebuilds the first two Advance Wars campaigns around colorful land, sea and air battles. Commanding officers bring personalities and special powers, while terrain, capture decisions and different unit roles provide a board-game-like tactical focus.
games.burden: Bright presentation does not remove the need to compare ranges, terrain, funds and matchups. It is turn-based, but particular mission conditions can still create strategic urgency. Nintendo's listed multiplayer includes versus play; do not assume a shared campaign. Hold behavior and readability require a check on the actual display.
games.first: Follow the early training and move one unit using its displayed information. Check whether the explanation makes its purpose clear before progressing to a larger force with several different roles to remember at once.
games.ruling: The colorful tactical collection offers commanding personalities and varied battles, with planning and controls still to assess. Our three service branches have achieved hydration and surrendered their ceremonial titles.
games.source_note: Nintendo identifies the Switch remake collection and turn-based land/sea/air tactics, terrain and CO powers. Versus multiplayer is confirmed; native campaign co-op is not established. No complete no-hold guarantee.
games.title: Advance Wars 1+2: Re-Boot Camp
games.quick_pitch: Explore rebuilt Advance Wars campaigns where colorful commanding officers and land, sea, and air units turn terrain into a tactical puzzle.
games.what_you_do: Follow training, inspect a unit's information, and choose movement, capture, or attack decisions while managing different battlefield roles and funds.
games.watch_for: Ranges, funds, and mission conditions still demand planning; versus multiplayer does not establish a shared campaign or comfortable controls.

games.case_title: Three Houses and None of Them Owns the Extension Cord
scene: Three Houses prompted me to divide the evening into noble houses. I gave Kit, Rae, and Velvet each a colored ribbon. Nia immediately asked which one she should wear.
“Whichever represents you.” “Several, Aiden.” “Then take several.” She did. My elegant taxonomy looked like a gift-wrapping accident within thirty seconds.
Remy wanted a crown on his ribbon. Mika wanted the colors to match the actual room map. Rosa asked whether the ribbons were washable because one had already landed in sauce.
Kit tied hers around a lamp so nobody borrowed it during rehearsal. Rae used hers to mark the repaired table leg. Velvet added hers to a costume where it looked intentional and expensive.
June said every house in 1967 had shared one extension cord. Dez corrected her: it belonged to Dez, and June had returned a lamp cord without a plug.
I removed the houses from the budget. Shawna kept one ribbon around my wrist. “So I can identify my wandering investment, nigga.”
games.pleasure: A teacher's relationship with students develops alongside tactical battles and a continent's political crisis. Choosing a house gives the long story a particular group to know, making friendships, loyalties and changing circumstances a substantial part of the experience.
games.burden: Normal difficulty with Casual mode revives fallen allies after battles, but it does not remove lessons, schedules, equipment or tactical menus. Monastery exploration adds three-dimensional movement and camera considerations. This is a rich character game with heavy management demands, not a simple visual novel because conversations are prominent.
games.first: Choose Normal and Casual for the first trial, then assess one introductory battle explanation and one conversation. Test monastery movement separately when available; comfort with selecting a battle square does not answer the camera question.
games.ruling: The long character story has appeal alongside tactical battles, while schedules, menus, and hub controls remain substantial. Our noble houses immediately became ribbons serving more useful purposes than classification.
games.source_note: Nintendo confirms turn-based battles, academy exploration/calendar and Normal/Casual options. Casual removes permanent allied losses in battle, not other complexity. Whole-path hold/camera comfort remains untested.
games.title: Fire Emblem: Three Houses
games.quick_pitch: Choose a house of characters to know over a long story, where relationships develop alongside tactical battles and a continent's political crisis.
games.what_you_do: Talk with the cast, manage lessons and equipment, explore the monastery, and command units through tactical battles in the chosen house's story.
games.watch_for: Normal/Casual reduces losses, but schedules and menus remain heavy; monastery movement adds a separate camera-control question.

games.case_title: The Emblem Is a Sticker on My Wallet
scene: Fire Emblem Engage made Remy ask whether our imaginary ministries could pair with legendary patrons. I said everyone could benefit from my sponsorship. Velvet placed a glittering sticker on my wallet.
“There. Legendary funding.”

Kit paired with Mercedes for an entrance-music arrangement. Rae paired with the hotel technician to stop a second table wobbling. Nia paired with a glass of wine and explicitly declared herself off duty for ten minutes.
I asked who wanted the Aiden emblem. Tank raised his hand, took my wallet, and paid the delivery man for the extra good crackers. My power activated immediately and with alarming efficiency.
June wanted a commemorative sticker for surviving both Blue Comet wars. Dez wanted one for surviving June. Remy made both by hand and gave them matching crowns.

Shawna recovered my wallet before I could sponsor a commemorative sticker kiosk. She peeled the glitter from the leather and pressed it onto my jacket. “There, baby. You can feel powerful without opening anything.”
games.pleasure: Engage emphasizes colorful tactical battles and the abilities gained by pairing characters with legendary Emblems. The appeal is experimenting with a cast's different strengths and seeing how a chosen pairing changes the possibilities on a grid-based battlefield.
games.burden: Weapon relationships, rings, skills and party development create many interlocking rules. Nintendo confirms Normal difficulty, Casual mode and Auto-Battle, plus a limited rewind system. Those aids change punishment or decision support; they do not prove low menu load or comfortable movement around the hub.
games.first: Use Normal and Casual, read one unit's weapon matchup, and try its basic action before exploring every ring combination. Examine Auto-Battle as an optional tool only after seeing what it controls, keeping the choice to participate or delegate yours.
games.ruling: The character pairings give this tactical adventure a distinct attraction, with its systems and movement questions retained. My legendary emblem currently grants allies access to the cracker budget.
games.source_note: Nintendo supports grid tactics, Emblem pairings, Normal/Casual, Auto-Battle and limited rewind. No full-path hold/camera assurance or shared campaign is inferred; multiplayer scope remains unverified here.
games.title: Fire Emblem Engage
games.quick_pitch: Experiment with character and Emblem pairings in colorful tactical battles, discovering how different strengths change the options available on the grid.
games.what_you_do: Read unit matchups, select battle actions, and develop characters through weapons, rings, skills, and pairings with legendary Emblems as the campaign progresses.
games.watch_for: Normal/Casual and other aids change punishment or support decisions; they do not establish low menu load or comfortable hub movement.

games.case_title: The Rabbids Have Applied for Cabinet Positions
scene: Mario and the Rabbids formed an unlikely tactical team. Our summit's unlikely team was Kit and Tank, who wanted the same stage platform for completely different reasons.
Kit wanted height for karaoke. Tank wanted to see whether the buffet had been replenished without standing. “Strategic awareness,” he said. Nigga had studied my vocabulary too well.
Rae inspected the platform and found it sturdy. Mika pointed out that moving it now would delay Velvet's rehearsal. A compromise formed: Kit could use it later, Tank could use his legs immediately.
Tank objected to the burden placed on the Ministry of Appetite. Rosa held up a fresh tray. The minister crossed the room at impressive speed.
Remy climbed onto the platform and tried a heroic pose. His crown tilted into one eye. Velvet straightened it, kissed his cheek, and asked him to stop dying before the opening number.
I proposed making them co-chairs. Shawna said we already had too many chairs and the next title would incur a storage fee.
games.pleasure: Mario characters and Rabbids join forces in colorful tactical battles, with each hero contributing a different role. The mismatch between earnest adventure and Rabbid behavior offers a comic frame for learning positioning, cover and coordinated attacks.
games.burden: Combat takes turns, but exploration, equipment and abilities still require learning and navigation. Nintendo describes local co-op as additional challenges, not the entire story campaign. Do not infer the sequel's hold toggles or other accommodations for this first game; exact gesture and camera comfort need checking.
games.first: Follow an early solo battle explanation and compare one movement option with one attack. If playing together is the main attraction, inspect the separate co-op challenges and their requirements rather than promising shared control of the whole campaign.
games.ruling: The mismatched cast gives the tactics a comic frame; the separate co-op challenges are not the campaign. Our unlikely coalition has resolved its platform dispute through the attraction of hot food.
games.source_note: Nintendo confirms turn-based combat and separate local co-op challenges. Co-op flag is restricted to those challenges; no whole-campaign co-op or Sparks of Hope control options are transferred.
games.title: Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle
games.quick_pitch: Join Mario characters and Rabbids in comic tactical battles, where their different roles make cover, positioning, and coordinated attacks worth learning.
games.what_you_do: Follow a solo battle explanation, compare movement with an attack, and learn exploration, equipment, and abilities as the adventure continues.
games.watch_for: Local co-op covers separate challenges, not the full campaign; navigation and controls need checking without assuming the sequel's accommodations.

games.case_title: The Planet of Unpaid Balloons
scene: Sparks of Hope sent its cast between imaginative planets. I had ordered three balloon planets to float over our budget table, each labeled with a proposed fund. The largest was HOST'S DISCRETION.
Rae turned it around. “This nigga gave himself Jupiter.” Nia laughed so suddenly her wine nearly joined the solar system.
Mika loved the planets and refused to let me claim their defense as support for the labels. They peeled off HOST'S DISCRETION and replaced it with an actual estimate of the remaining room charge.
The label barely fit. Kit requested a smaller planet for stage lighting. Velvet asked whether her fee had become a moon because she preferred money that didn't orbit somebody else's priorities.
Remy found a marker and drew a crown on the nearest tiny satellite. June and Dez argued about who had discovered the planet of borrowed jackets first.
Shawna cut the string to my enormous balloon and handed it to me. “Hold your discretionary spending.” Nigga, I spent the entire discussion physically attached to a bad decision.
games.pleasure: Mario and the Rabbids travel between imaginative planets, meeting odd characters and combining heroes with helpful Sparks. Tactical battles sit inside a larger exploratory adventure, with the cast's antics providing a light comic reason to see what the next place contains.
games.burden: Ubisoft documents specific hold toggles, single-press alternatives, camera adjustments, automatic skill management and invulnerability. These are real options, not proof of a wholly no-rush path: direct movement, camera handling and airborne or traversal actions need checking. The first game's co-op challenges do not establish co-op here.
games.first: Inspect those control options before play, then test ordinary movement and a first battle at the preferred difficulty. Check how a team jump or other moving action feels when introduced; stop there if the practical demands outweigh the appeal.
games.ruling: The colorful planetary journey has comic appeal, with movement, camera, and update details still important. Our budget's largest planet is currently tethered to the man who named it after himself.
games.source_note: Developer UX interview documents listed options and time to think during turns; publisher article confirms direct real-time movement. These do not verify every traversal sequence. Single-player sequel assessed separately from Kingdom Battle.
games.title: Mario + Rabbids Sparks of Hope
games.quick_pitch: Travel between imaginative planets with Mario and the Rabbids, combining heroes with Sparks while their antics give each new place comic appeal.
games.what_you_do: Explore with direct movement, inspect control options, and choose hero abilities or battle actions while learning how movement-based techniques work.
games.watch_for: Useful control options exist, but camera, direct movement, and traversal still need testing; the first game's co-op does not transfer.

games.case_title: The Alien Invasion Has a Delivery Window
scene: XCOM's headquarters needed research, equipment, and people ready for a crisis. Our headquarters received a delivery marked EXTRATERRESTRIAL WELCOME EFFECT. I asked the driver whether he had the correct room.
He showed me my signature. Tank said, “Nigga, the aliens know who summoned them.”

Inside were silver inflatable creatures intended for the entrance. Kit wanted one behind the karaoke stage. Mika wanted all three above the registration desk. Rae wanted to know whether either improvement was worth the charge.
Nia asked which items could still be returned. The driver pointed to the unopened boxes. Everyone looked at the creature I had already inflated halfway while pretending to investigate it.
Shawna let the air out. The alien collapsed slowly against my chest, an intimate portrait of fiscal surrender. Velvet photographed only after asking, and I agreed because it was admittedly excellent.
We kept one for the show and returned two. The invasion was contained. Its surviving diplomat received a feather boa and a supporting role, neither authorized by its home planet.

games.case_title: The Resistance Has Occupied the Photo Booth
scene: XCOM 2's resistance put ideas into Porsche's head. She and Mercedes took over the sponsor photo booth after its operator insisted every photograph needed his bottle in the foreground.
“He bought the backdrop,” I said. “He didn't buy my face,” Mercedes said.

Velvet joined them with the surviving inflatable alien. Remy supplied a crown. The booth rapidly produced a series of excellent pictures in which the sponsor's product appeared nowhere except accidentally beneath a chair.
I approached as mediator. Porsche handed me a plain backdrop cloth and asked me to hold one corner. The resistance had conscripted its supposedly neutral observer.
Kit adjusted the light. Rae took Nia's picture, then let Nia take hers. Neither called it anything more significant than a photograph, which was why I was absolutely forbidden to provide commentary.

The sponsor accepted the alternate setup after Velvet offered a separately priced product shot. Nigga, the occupation ended through commercial negotiation, while I remained holding the cloth because everyone liked the angle.

games.case_title: The Corporate Spy Wants the Dessert Password
scene: Invisible, Inc.'s corporate espionage made me suspicious of a locked catering cart. Rosa told me it contained dessert and would open when dessert was supposed to open.
Tank studied the latch. “Any agents available?” Rae pointed at the schedule. “Your extraction window's in twenty minutes.”

I offered to negotiate early access for senior leadership. Shawna asked whether leadership intended to eat dinner first. I said this was reconnaissance. She removed the dessert fork from my hand with considerable expertise.

Nia and Kit were discussing the actual security deposit. Kit wanted the hotel to acknowledge the condition of its lamps before anyone moved them. Nia approved the idea and asked Porsche to photograph the equipment.
While we handled useful corporate intelligence, Tank asked Rosa directly whether there were extra strawberries in the kitchen. There were. She brought him a bowl because it didn't disturb service.
Nigga completed the mission by knowing a person's name and asking a normal question. I was still explaining my stealth plan to a woman married to it.

games.case_title: The Mage Has Read the Catering Contract
scene: Shadowrun Returns mixed magic and corporate trouble. I suggested our financial committee needed a mage. Nia asked whether a mage could make my personal purchases stop appearing under SHARED EXPENSES.
“That's advanced magic,” Tank said. “Nigga's been practicing for years.”
Rae found the charge for monogrammed tool rolls. I had bought them to honor her table repair. She stared at the initials. They were mine.
“It's a summit gift.” “Then why does it say AIDEN?” “Brand continuity.”

Velvet took one look and offered to use a roll for makeup brushes if I stopped calling it a diplomatic gesture. Remy wanted another for cables. Actual people found useful purposes while the corporation's founder struggled with its reputation.

Shawna drew a line through SHARED and wrote PERSONAL beneath the charge. Nia approved the classification without billing us for sorcery. Rae kept the plain tool roll she'd brought from home, tightened one final screw, and left my branding on the table where it belonged.

games.case_title: The Crew Has Conditions for Taking My Job
scene: Dragonfall's crew had histories and loyalties. I recruited our own crew for a dangerous mission: persuade the hotel to refund the duplicate chair delivery. Everybody wanted to know the terms.
Rae wanted me present so I couldn't summarize the conversation afterward. Nia wanted a time limit on how long she'd spend helping. Kit wanted the promised lamp left untouched during the expedition.

Tank wanted food. Velvet wanted us back before her rehearsal. Remy wanted to perform his fanfare when we succeeded. We had not yet approached the manager and already possessed six competing victory conditions.
Shawna assembled the relevant receipts. She handed them to me, then made me read the first sentence of my own cancellation request aloud. It contained an apology and no mention of destiny.

The manager refunded the unopened chairs minus the stated fee. Rae accepted the result. Nia reclaimed her evening. Remy played two tasteful seconds before remembering his promise to be ridiculous and adding three gloriously unnecessary more.
Nigga, the crew had earned its ending. I had earned a smaller bill.

games.case_title: The Matrix Password Is Under the Ice Bucket
scene: Shadowrun's Hong Kong crew faced a dense world of intrigue. Our immediate intrigue concerned the sponsor's tablet, which contained the itemized charges and refused to open without a code.
I announced we would need a hacker. Mika lifted the ice bucket. The code was on a card beneath it. “We need a dry card.”
Nia read the charges while Rae held a napkin against the wet corner. Velvet found a proposed fee for using her stage name in a sponsor slideshow. She asked who had decided that was a benefit to her.
The sponsor called it promotional synergy. Remy made a sad little keyboard noise. Mercedes asked him to repeat it under the phrase, which improved the presentation enormously.
We removed the unapproved slide. Velvet offered a separate rate if the sponsor wanted her involvement. He declined, and everybody survived the absence of synergy.
I tried locking the tablet dramatically at the end. It played a cheerful confirmation sound. Nigga, our cyberpunk operation concluded like somebody successfully setting a kitchen timer.

games.case_title: The Hero Has Acquired an Unflattering Nickname
scene: Wildermyth's ordinary people could develop extraordinary histories. Remy asked whether the summit would remember him as King Receipts the Glorious. Velvet said it depended on how many fanfares he attempted before dinner.
Tank nominated me as Aiden the Charged. June preferred Aiden of the Many Deposits. Dez said my legend needed fewer syllables and more shame.
I tried naming my own heroic transformation: the Unifier. Rae looked at the budget balloons. “The Inflator.” Nia laughed, then apologized without sounding sorry.

Kit wanted a better title too. She proposed Keeper of the Entrance Light. Mercedes granted it immediately, along with responsibility for remembering where she'd put her glasses. The hero checked her head before searching anywhere else.
Shawna leaned into me. “I like the man before his titles.” I whispered something suitably promising about his other talents. She smiled and reminded him of the evening's private appointment.
My legend improved. No proclamation followed. The Unifier had discovered that a quiet sentence could outperform a rented banner when addressed to the correct woman.

games.case_title: The Mercenary Company Has a Snack Clause
scene: Wartales' working company made Rosa examine our catering agreement like a mercenary captain. She wanted clear hours, sufficient staff, and nobody treating the kitchen as a magical room that generated plates.
I said I respected the craft. She pointed at the overtime request. “Then respect it numerically.”

Rae backed her, partly on principle and partly because the replacement crackers had transformed her opinion of the summit. Kit wanted the staff to have a break before her karaoke turn so they could enjoy themselves if they wished.
Nia drafted one clean payment line. Her handwriting looked like a decorative threat. Mika typed it while she read aloud, preserving the actual words and mercifully abandoning the penmanship.
Darnell approached with a vague proposal involving a yacht chef. Rosa asked for a name and a rate. He had neither. Tank escorted his nigga toward a plate before the proposal developed further.
We funded the staff hours. The company secured its contract, and I gained no heroic title beyond the name already printed on my card.

games.case_title: The Brothers Demand a Contract Before the Toast
scene: Battle Brothers' mercenary company attracted June. “Everybody signs before anybody carries anything,” she said. Dez raised an eyebrow. “Look at the Blue Comet discovering contracts.”

June and Dez inspected their two-sided copies of the 1967 agreement. Both signatures were undeniable now. June insisted signatures only mattered if promises were kept. Dez inspected the alternating-song clause and suggested June had spent fifty-nine years negotiating with the fucking jukebox.
I offered a toast to old alliances. Velvet asked whether the current deposit had cleared. Nia checked the confirmation. It hadn't. The toast waited while I found the correct message on my phone.
Rae and Kit compared the actual staffing numbers. Remy brought Velvet water because she had stopped talking and that worried him more than her talking ever did.
The confirmation arrived. Velvet relaxed, thanked him, and accepted the glass. June raised hers. Dez raised hers too, without conceding the jacket claim.
Nigga, we had an alliance with conditions, which looked a lot like an ordinary agreement between people intending to remain friends after the evening cost money.

scene: BATTLETECH's enormous machines made my mechanical photo throne look almost restrained. I said so. Rae crouched beside its bent footrest and asked whether restraint included the repair charge.
“It came like that.” Shawna found the photograph of me standing on it. “It came considerably flatter.”

Mika loved the chair's ridiculous silhouette. They suggested using it motionless in a corner for photographs. The hotel technician disconnected the troublesome mechanism, leaving a perfectly decent seat inside an absurd shell.

Remy climbed in and looked magnificent until his crown caught the top edge. Velvet removed the crown, sat on the broad arm, and told the photographer to proceed. Two professionals salvaged the machine through superior positioning.

I asked for a solo picture. Tank sat in my lap before the camera flashed. “Crew portrait, nigga.” The photograph contained two grown men, one enormous chair, and my expression discovering new dimensions of regret.
Rae taped a note over the control: OFF. Nia added the repair estimate to my personal column. Our mercenary machine had returned from battle with an itemized history.

games.case_title: The Scales of Conviction Prefer Actual Dinner

“Nigga, affirm it with a plate.”

Kit wanted a vegetarian option kept clearly marked. Rae wanted the olives replenished. Remy wanted time to eat before his costume change. These requests required three practical adjustments, not an election between hungry people.

Mercedes offered to play a short instrumental echo during the break, which June accepted because she liked the arrangement and Dez accepted because nobody had to stand through the whole song again.

games.case_title: The Noble Class Has Lost Its Drink Tokens
scene: The Ivalice story's class conflict made Rae examine the gold and silver drink tokens I'd ordered. I explained that gold represented summit leadership. She asked who had appointed it.
I looked at my own handful of gold. Nigga, evidence can be very loud without making a sound.

games.case_title: The Time Loop Has Replayed My Card Decline
scene: Cobalt Core's crew faced a time-loop mystery. Our crew faced the payment terminal returning to the same cheerful screen every time I tapped my card. Tank began narrating the recurrence.
“Again the captain confronts his destiny.” “Nigga, stop.” “Again destiny requests another method.”

The card wasn't declined; the reader had lost connection. Mika found the floor manager while Nia checked that we weren't approving duplicate charges. Rae moved the cable away from a chair wheel and discovered the practical villain.
Shawna stood beside me without making a joke, which was suspiciously loving under the circumstances. I thanked her. “Don't thank me yet. I'm saving it for when the room's quieter.”

The next attempt worked. Velvet's remaining deposit was confirmed, and she relaxed her shoulders in a way I hadn't noticed she'd been holding them. Remy brought her the confirmation without a fanfare.
I asked Tank to retire the narration. He nodded solemnly. “The captain has escaped the loop.” Nigga added applause, and several traitors joined him.

games.burden: Crew decks, ship layout, incoming fire and upgrades create interacting information to track. The publisher invites play at one's own pace, but gesture comfort and the complete sequence of encounters are not independently tested. This is a card-driven tactical game, not a reflex flying game, yet it still requires attentive planning.

games.ruling: The crew and time-loop mystery give these spaceship card battles personality, with interacting systems still substantial. Our payment loop ended through a cable repair and a carefully checked confirmation.

games.case_title: The Frost Counter Is on the Dessert Table
scene: Wildfrost's visible counters made me obsess over the dessert station. A little card told staff when to bring out the chilled trays. I asked whether it represented our remaining turns before catastrophe.
Rosa read it. “It represents dessert.”

Tank wanted to speed up the sequence. Rae wanted him to stop hovering over the good crackers while pretending to care about temperature. Nia passed Rae the bowl and received a smile that had nothing to do with fiscal policy.

Kit marked her rehearsal break on the schedule so it wouldn't collide with service. Mercedes agreed to test the final quiet passage earlier. Two small changes made the evening feel less like a set of people waiting to interrupt one another.

I offered an emergency countdown display. Mika said the existing card was perfectly adequate. June told me the Blue Comet had managed with Dez shouting from the kitchen. Dez said June had usually ignored that system too.
The trays arrived. Nobody froze, nothing exploded, and the coalition survived without acquiring another screen showing numbers I intended to misunderstand.

games.burden: The counters measure turns until actions, not a requirement to click within seconds. Even so, attack order, positioning, status effects and companion survival can be demanding, and a cute appearance does not predict an easy run. Card placement gestures and all-path input comfort remain checks rather than verified assurances.

games.case_title: Fifty-One Games and One Agreed Expense Sheet
scene: Clubhouse Games offered a collection of small possibilities. I tried proposing fifty-one corresponding summit committees. Shawna took the pen out of my hand before committee number two could acquire stationery.
Rae selected a familiar board game for a short break. Nia sat beside her to watch, then asked to take the next turn when it came around. Nobody made a declaration about what this meant.

Kit and Remy compared the in-game explanations while Velvet checked the now confirmed show payment. Rosa put the final catering total beside it. Mika added the room charge and circled the modest reserve.

June and Dez agreed that their separate jacket arrangement belonged in their own handwriting, however much Nia's legal-looking paper tempted them. Their settlement didn't require everyone else to inherit the 1967 jukebox dispute.
I approved the financial sheet. It wasn't the final coalition treaty, merely numbers we understood and commitments we could honor. Tank applauded once, with his hands safely away from food.
“Historic, nigga.” I bowed. Shawna pulled me into the empty chair before history ordered another banner.

interludes.title: Both Sides of the Paper and Who Gets Paid to Hold It
paragraphs: Nia unfolded the old Blue Comet invoice during the break. June pointed at the front. “My signature. The other party refused.” Dez turned it over. “My signature. The other party refused.”
Nobody spoke for three beautiful seconds. Then Tank put his face in his hands.
“Niggas. Turn the fucking paper over.”

They had each spent fifty-nine years looking at the surface that supported their argument. June had signed the hall charge. Dez had signed the peace terms on the reverse. Both signatures were there, along with alternating jukebox selections, return of June's jacket before winter, and two ginger ales that had survived every retelling by remaining unmentioned.

I reached for my phone to photograph the breakthrough. Shawna said I could ask first. Both veterans agreed, provided I kept the picture out of any slideshow containing my face. Apparently they'd read the conditions of my hospitality more carefully than their own peace agreement.

June studied the jacket clause. Dez studied the ginger ales. Each had located a different obstacle to victory. Remy offered a two-sided fanfare. Velvet put a hand over his keyboard. “Let these women experience the silence, baby. They paid fifty-nine years for it.”

The present-day hotel invoice waited beside the historical one. Kit had found a duplicate lamp charge. Rae had found a labor line that assumed she'd remain available to repair furniture all evening. Nia had found herself listed as legal support through midnight. None of those entries had been agreed with the people whose time they described.
I said the hotel must have misunderstood. Rae turned the page toward me. The note read PER HOST REQUEST. My handwriting, for once, was entirely legible.
“Nigga, you can't call my hands a resource before you ask whether they're free.”

I began explaining that I'd meant available in case something went wrong. “Something already went wrong,” she said. “You spent my evening.” Her voice was sharper than it had been over the crackers, and it should have been. This wasn't a preference about olives. I had given somebody else a claim on her time because she had been helpful in front of me.
Kit said she could take some of the work. Rae shook her head. “The work isn't yours to redistribute either. Start with the assumption that I came to play.”

I saw Nia close her folder. She'd been trying to do that for twenty minutes. I had interpreted each new useful answer as an invitation to produce another question. A free lawyer was becoming one of my favorite features of the room, which was an ugly way to think about a woman who had come partly because she liked the mechanic sitting beside her.

I crossed out both assignments. The correction didn't make the earlier presumption clever. Nia kept the folder closed and said she would join the rest of the conversation as a person, which I considered a remarkably modest demand under the circumstances.

The sponsor approached before we could enjoy our breakthrough. He wanted a photograph with the coalition's respectable leadership before the performers changed into their show clothes. He nodded toward Kit and me, then looked at Velvet's headpiece as though it might damage his insurance.

Kit asked what he meant by respectable. He said polished, professional, welcoming to everyone. Velvet lifted her payment schedule. “I'm a professional. Welcoming everyone is already in the room. Which part of my head costs you customers?”

The man laughed because he wanted it to be a joke. It wasn't only a joke. Remy stood beside her in ordinary clothes, crown in hand, waiting to learn which version of him the sponsor considered sellable. Nobody at the table had volunteered to become the decorative proof that money could get along with difference if difference selected a quieter outfit.

I offered to take the photograph later. Shawna looked at me. “Later with whom?” I had tried delaying the choice without changing it. My skill at mediation often consisted of moving a bad sentence ten minutes into the future and hoping nobody followed.
The sponsor left to take a call. Kit exhaled. “I could do the picture and insist the show stays exactly as planned. It might keep the money uncomplicated.”
Rae looked at her. “Uncomplicated for whom?”

Kit was tired of that question, which didn't make it the wrong one. “For the people getting paid. Sometimes I've kept a library event alive by letting a donor feel like the room looked familiar. I'm not proud of every conversation. I also don't want the performers losing a fee because I chose the cleanest speech.”

Kit looked at me before continuing. “And don't decide the person who can write a check is the bravest one here. My library hours got cut. I can't replace a lost fee out of my account. That affects what risks feel available.” I had been preparing a generous expression; it became uncomfortable on my face. Rae nodded. “I believe you. It still matters whose face the sponsor chose for professional.” Kit said yes, both things mattered. Neither sentence paid the fee. We still had to find the money, and my advantages were about to become useful only if I stopped treating them as a superior moral personality.

Velvet nodded once. “That's a real problem. Here's my real answer: ask me before you purchase my survival with a smaller version of me.” She wasn't rejecting every negotiation. She wanted the person whose work was being negotiated to exist inside it. “I can choose an outfit for a client. I can also say the client's request costs more than the booking's worth. Don't make that choice and hand me the money like you rescued me.”

Remy said the sponsor had called his act surprisingly tasteful. “I know what he meant. I also know my act contains a pun about a royal accountant getting double-entry heartbreak. Tasteful wasn't a review. It was relief.”
Velvet laughed despite herself. “That joke is so fucking bad.” “And yet it belongs to me.” He put his crown on, crooked again. She left it crooked for once.

Rae described the hotel entrance earlier: Kit received a question about lighting, Rae received directions for contractors. Kit had initially explained the difference away because she hadn't wanted the room to become unpleasant before the party started. “I made the pleasant version more important than the thing you said happened,” Kit said now. Rae nodded. She didn't make Kit perform an apology twice just to prolong the advantage.

June leaned forward. “Money doesn't ask all of us to become respectable in the same way. But don't use that sentence to tell me I've never wanted a nice suit or a calm evening. I like both. This suit is beautiful.” Dez touched her sleeve. “It is. And this time it's actually on its owner.”

June let the laugh settle. “I've swallowed things at work to keep wages coming. I've also said no and worried afterward. I don't need my younger self put on trial by people who got to read the ending before deciding what she'd do.” She looked at me. “Your room needs choices. It doesn't need a purity competition sponsored by your wallet.”

I had been quietly imagining myself funding a perfect space where none of this occurred. That fantasy flattered the payer. It also made every complication somebody else's failure to appreciate the gift. I could rent chairs. I could pay staff. I couldn't make a Black woman's account of what happened at the door unnecessary just by paying for a nicer door.

Nia asked whether we could keep two questions visible: what immediate arrangement a person chose, and what conditions made the choice expensive. “I don't want my own compromises used to tell the next person they're obligated to make them. I also don't want a room full of spectators grading whether I resisted attractively enough.” Then she opened her hands. “That's my contribution. Somebody else can type it if they want it remembered.”

Mika typed. They also admitted they'd nearly accepted the sponsor's photograph request because they wanted the event to start and the room to look successful. “A beautiful room can photograph a problem out of existence,” they said. “I'm very good at that. I'd like to be good at knowing when I'm doing it.”

Kit asked about putting the cost somewhere visible. What would it take to keep the promised fees independent of the sponsor's flattering photograph? This time she asked Velvet first. Velvet named the amount already contracted, not a moral price. Rosa named the staffing balance. The hotel manager confirmed which duplicate and unopened rentals could be refunded. Numbers replaced the vague threat that honesty would bankrupt the evening.

Darnell arrived asking whether his party supplies qualified as entertainment expense. Tank glanced at the bag he'd been carrying. “Your cocaine is not a coalition department, nigga.” Darnell took it away and returned with a plate, where his contribution could remain the size of his appetite. We did not need his procurement story to understand the difference between an agreed fee and a personal decision.

I covered the contracted shortfall, approved the refunds, and told the sponsor the photograph would include whoever independently wanted to be in it. Nobody owed a performance of gratitude. He could choose whether he wanted the photograph on those terms. The room did not instantly become just. It became a room where one particular leverage attempt had failed without its target losing her fee.

Kit kept the duplicate-charge note. Rae kept her evening. Nia stayed seated instead of reopening the folder. June and Dez requested copies of both sides of their invoice and agreed to split the ancient ginger-ale debt symbolically over dinner. No interest. No tribunal. No commemorative eagle.

I offered the eagle at a discount. Shawna kissed my cheek, took my pencil, and said, “The survivors have suffered enough.” Then she asked me to dance later as her husband, without representing any ministry. Nigga, I accepted before somebody could turn the offer into a job description.

ending.title: The Money Is Agreed and the Furniture Is Still an Argument
paragraphs: The financial sheet fit on one page when we stopped describing every expense as a historic investment. Performer payments. Staff time. Room charge. Equipment already in place. A small reserve for things that genuinely broke, distinct from things I became excited about while walking past a rental catalogue. Nia read the categories aloud. Rae checked the numbers against the receipts. Kit caught a duplicated lamp charge and looked so satisfied that I almost ordered a small trophy before remembering the entire fucking meeting.

Velvet received the confirmation she'd been waiting for. She put her phone away and became interested in the room again. Remy offered his arm. They went to check the microphone together, discussing a deliberately terrible pun he intended to put into the introduction. She said it was awful. He said that was its function. She agreed it performed its function flawlessly.

Rosa confirmed the additional staff time and went to speak with the kitchen. Mercedes and Porsche checked the recording schedule against the show order. Mika marked the approved equipment on the miniature floor plan, then looked at the actual doorway and frowned. The budget was intelligible. The rooms still required work. I had mistaken paying for square footage for knowing what to do with it, a confusion apparently common among niggas wearing ceremonial jackets indoors.

June and Dez kept their copied invoice in a plain envelope. Both sides. June wrote TURN OVER on the front in enormous letters. Dez wrote SAME TO YOU on the back. Their private jacket arrangement included looking for the old alteration pattern and having dinner afterward. The original jacket remained with Dez for the moment, which June permitted while describing herself as extraordinarily patient. Dez called this a promising new direction in historical fiction.

Nobody signed the final coalition charter. We had agreed financial terms, confirmed immediate payments, and recorded unresolved decorative claims for later review. I remained optimistic about those claims because optimism is cheap until you arrange a spotlight for it. Shawna read the little unresolved line, looked at me, and said nothing. Marriage contains silences with the tensile strength of steel.

Nia put the pen down. Rae asked whether she'd like a little air before the next room. Nia said yes before making it sound more considered. Kit handed them the room map, then noticed she'd given them her karaoke list instead. Everybody laughed, including Kit. She retrieved the list and told them the good balcony was marked on the actual map, which Mika still needed to verify. Even flirtation had encountered our venue problem.

I watched them leave and kept every helpful suggestion inside my own head. Shawna noticed. She linked her arm through mine. “You can learn.” I whispered that I possessed several advanced qualifications she hadn't examined tonight. “Then stop enrolling yourself in committees.” Her smile gave my future a much more interesting shape than the financial statement.

Tank carried the budget into the next room. Mika followed with the model hotel. June and Dez continued arguing fondly about whether alternating songs meant one each or whichever one sounded better. The Second Great War had survived its treasury meeting. Its armies now needed somewhere sensible to sit, and I was about to discover that a room could be expensive in ways a receipt didn't explain.
